sample.task: Write in simple and short way like summarize it: Just as arguers can stealthily replace an opponent’s proposition by one that is easier to attack, they can replace their own proposition with one that is easier to defendThey can claim that no Scotsman puts sugar on his porridge, and when confronted with Angus, who puts sugar on his porridge, say this shows that Angus is not a true Scotsman. The no true Scotsman fallacy also explains why no true Christian ever kills, no true communist state is repressive,One can always maintain a belief, no matter what it is, by saying that the burden of proof is on those who disagree Bertrand Russell responded to this fallacy when he was challenged to explain why he was an atheist rather than an agnostic, since he could not prove that God does not exist. He replied, “Nobody can prove that there is not between the Earth and Mars a china teapot revolving in an elliptic orbit.”argument from authority. The authority being deferred to is often religious, as in the gospel song and bumper sticker “God said it, I believe it, that settles it.” But it can also be political or academic. Intellectual cliques often revolve around a guru whose pronouncements become secular gospelappeal to emotion: “How can anyone look at this photo of the grieving parents of a dead child and say that war deaths have declined?” And the increasingly popular affective fallacy, in which a statement may be rejected if it is “hurtful” or “harmful” or may cause “discomfort.”A related tactic is the genetic fallacy, which has nothing to do with DNA but is related to the words “genesis” and “generate.” It refers to evaluating an idea not by its truth but by its origins.
sample.chosen: This passage discusses various logical fallacies used in arguments. The "No True Scotsman" fallacy involves modifying a claim to exclude any counterexamples, like saying no true Scotsman puts sugar on porridge and dismissing exceptions as not true Scotsmen. The "burden of proof" fallacy maintains a belief by insisting others disprove it, as Bertrand Russell's teapot analogy illustrates. The "appeal to authority" fallacy defers to an authority figure, often religious, political, or academic. The "appeal to emotion" fallacy uses emotional manipulation, while the "affective fallacy" rejects statements causing discomfort. Lastly, the "genetic fallacy" judges an idea based on its origin rather than its merit.
sample.rejected: The no true Scotsman fallacy is a logical error where someone challenges a proposition by claiming that the other person is not actually making the proposition they claim they are. This fallacy can be used to challenge any argument by claiming that the other person is not really making their case.
